# Preface {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## In one paragraph

A rigorous, self-contained path from undergraduate mathematics to a
production-grade Bayesian **Marketing Mix Model** — built from scratch, deriving
the math instead of calling a library. You assemble the whole stack yourself:
regression → Bayesian inference → MCMC → optimization → a dynamic,
causally-calibrated MMM → the software engineering to ship it. If you have ever
run an MMM framework and wanted to know *why* it works — and where it quietly
misleads you — this is that book.
:::

This is a self-contained textbook on the mathematics and the software engineering
that underlie modern **Marketing Mix Modeling (MMM)**. It takes you from standard
quantitative prerequisites all the way to advanced practice — without hand-waving,
and without assuming you already know Bayesian modeling, MCMC, causal inference,
or constrained optimization.

**What you will be able to do.**

- Build a full Bayesian MMM end-to-end — from the data-generating process through
  prior elicitation and MCMC inference to budget optimization.
- *Calibrate* that model against experiments, so its budget recommendations rest
  on causal evidence rather than on a curve the observational data can't pin down.
- Engineer the whole thing into a reproducible, testable, trustworthy system.

**What makes it different.** It is theory-first. Most MMM material shows you which
library functions to call; this book derives the mathematics so you understand
what those functions assume, when they break, and how to fix them — including the
causal calibration step most treatments skip entirely.

## Who this book is for

You will get the most out of this book if you arrive with:

- **Calculus** — derivatives, integrals, sequences and series.
- **Linear algebra** — vectors, matrices, solving linear systems.
- **Calculus-based statistics** — random variables, expectation, common
  distributions, the idea of a likelihood.
- **Mathematical maturity** — comfort reading and writing short proofs, of the
  kind built in discrete mathematics, an introduction-to-proofs /
  mathematical-structures course, or real analysis. The book proves results where
  the proof is illuminating; you should be willing to follow and reproduce them.

You will leave able to reason about — and build — a full Bayesian MMM: from the
data-generating process, through prior elicitation and MCMC inference, to budget
optimization grounded in experiments you can actually trust, and the software
engineering that makes such a system reproducible.

## How the book is organized

```{python}
#| label: fig-learning-path
#| fig-cap: "The learning path. Each part builds strictly on the ones before it. The turn from Part V to Part VI — from *building* the model to *trusting* it — is the book's intellectual spine."
#| fig-align: center
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch

FOUND = "#3b6ea5"  # foundations (Parts I–IV)
CORE = "#c1654f"   # the MMM core (Parts V–VI)
ENG = "#5f7a6b"    # engineering & capstone (Parts VII–VIII)
PRE = "#8a9099"    # prerequisites

rows = [
    ("Prerequisites", PRE, True),
    ("Part I · Mathematical Foundations", FOUND, False),
    ("Part II · Regression & Bayesian Inference", FOUND, False),
    ("Part III · Computation: Sampling (MCMC / HMC)", FOUND, False),
    ("Part IV · Optimization", FOUND, False),
    ("Part V · Marketing Mix Modeling: Modeling", CORE, False),
    ("Part VI · Causal Grounding & Calibration", CORE, False),
    ("Part VII · Software Engineering & Computer Science", ENG, False),
    ("Part VIII · Capstone", ENG, False),
]
PRE_DETAIL = "calculus · linear algebra · calculus-based statistics · proof literacy"

n = len(rows)
bw, bh, gap = 9.0, 0.68, 0.28
fig_h = n * (bh + gap) + 0.4
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, fig_h))
ax.set_xlim(0, 10)
ax.set_ylim(0, fig_h)
ax.axis("off")

cx = 5.0
ys = []
y = fig_h - 0.2 - bh
for label, color, is_pre in rows:
    ys.append(y)
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch(
        (cx - bw / 2, y), bw, bh,
        boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.09",
        linewidth=0, facecolor=color))
    if is_pre:
        ax.text(cx, y + bh * 0.66, label, ha="center", va="center",
                color="white", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
        ax.text(cx, y + bh * 0.30, PRE_DETAIL, ha="center", va="center",
                color="white", fontsize=8.5)
    else:
        ax.text(cx, y + bh / 2, label, ha="center", va="center",
                color="white", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
    y -= (bh + gap)

for i in range(n - 1):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(
        (cx, ys[i]), (cx, ys[i + 1] + bh),
        arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=13, linewidth=1.4, color="#444"))

i_v = 5  # Part V → Part VI
y_mid = (ys[i_v] + (ys[i_v + 1] + bh)) / 2
ax.text(cx + bw / 2 + 0.15, y_mid, "build → trust", ha="left", va="center",
        fontsize=9.5, style="italic", color=CORE, fontweight="bold")

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The book runs **foundations → applications**. Each part builds strictly on the
ones before it.

- **Part I — Mathematical Foundations.** Linear algebra, multivariable calculus
  (gradient, Jacobian, Hessian), and probability/statistics, pitched to be
  reactivated quickly and then extended.
- **Part II — Regression & Bayesian Inference.** From ordinary least squares to
  Bayesian and hierarchical regression.
- **Part III — Computation: Sampling.** Markov chains, MCMC, and Hamiltonian
  Monte Carlo / NUTS — the engine that actually fits the models — and how to tell
  a good fit from a broken one.
- **Part IV — Optimization.** Convexity, linear programming (with duality and
  shadow prices), and constrained nonlinear optimization via SLSQP.
- **Part V — Marketing Mix Modeling: Modeling.** Adstock, saturation, fitting,
  and dynamic (state-space) models, through to budget optimization — the best
  *observational* MMM you can build.
- **Part VI — Causal Grounding & Calibration.** Why that observational model is
  untrustworthy for the decision you built it for — causal inference,
  quasi-experimental designs, calibrating the response curve to experiments, and
  accumulating that evidence into a reusable prior store.
- **Part VII — Software Engineering & Computer Science.** The engineering — from
  CS first principles to architecture, data engineering, and testing — that turns
  the math into a reliable system.
- **Part VIII — Capstone.** A worked, end-to-end engagement on synthetic data.

The mathematics starts at the undergraduate level and ramps up toward advanced
master's / first-year-PhD rigor as the book progresses. Where a result is
genuinely illuminating we prove it; where a proof is mechanical we cite it.

## How to use this book

Each chapter follows the same rhythm: **intuition → theory and proofs → worked
examples → a runnable code tie-in → exercises → a summary**. The exercises come
in four escalating tiers:

- **C — Conceptual / reading comprehension.**
- **B — By hand** (compute or derive manually).
- **P — Prove it** (short, useful proofs).
- **A — Applied / code.**

Worked solutions live in a single appendix at the very back of the book, with no
inline links from the exercises. This is deliberate: reach for them only after a
real attempt. (Instructor builds can render the full solutions; reader builds can
omit them entirely.)

Every chapter closes with a **Summary**: the handful of concepts you must be able
to state and the key identities you should be able to reproduce from memory before
moving on. Treat it as a self-check and a quick reference to come back to.

## Reproducibility

Code in this book is original and self-contained — minimal PyMC / SciPy snippets
that teach the same patterns a production MMM uses, with no proprietary source,
firm priors, or client data. Pinned dependencies live in `requirements.txt`. Heavy
sampling cells are cached via Quarto's `freeze`, so the book renders quickly and
reproducibly.

## Canonical sources

Every field in this book is anchored to its canonical references — Strang and
Axler for linear algebra; Casella & Berger for statistics; Gelman et al. (BDA3),
Gelman & Hill, and McElreath for Bayesian modeling; Robert & Casella, Neal, and
Betancourt for MCMC/HMC; Boyd & Vandenberghe, Bertsimas & Tsitsiklis, and
Nocedal & Wright for optimization; Imbens & Rubin and Angrist & Pischke for causal
inference and quasi-experimental design; and the published MMM literature
(Jin et al.) for the application. Full citations are in the bibliography.
